newsitem.title: USA: Scientists see signs of universe's "missing matter".
newsitem.headline: Scientists see signs of universe's "missing matter".

text.p: At least some of the universe's missing matter appears to consist of hydrogen and helium gas floating between the galaxies, Johns Hopkins University researchers reported on Sunday.

In an article in the April 20 issue of the Astrophysics Journal, the scientists said the thinly spread gas consisted of atoms of the two elements. These atoms had been stripped of their electrons, or "ionized," by intense radiation early in the formation of the universe.

This gas probably accounted for much of the ordinary, or "baryonic," matter that has not been able to be detected in the universe. But it does not include the more exotic types of matter that scientists believe make up a majority of all matter in the universe, the university said in a statement.
"We now believe we can say how much intergalactic gas, baryonic material, there must have been," Johns Hopkins astrophysicist Arthur F. Davidsen said in the statement.

Scientists have long suspected that as-yet unseen matter was in the universe, because not enough matter has been found in stars and galaxies to be consistent with "Big Bang" theories of how the universe began billions of years ago.
The Johns Hopkins researchers based their findings on analyses of previous astronomical observations.

They said the early universe may have contained a "continuous medium" of hydrogen and helium gases, with regions of higher and lower density blending together smoothly, rather than more disctinct clouds as previous theories have held.
